title.title: The Solomon–Yau least-volume conjecture
title.subtitle: Claim: after the equator, the least-volume minimal hypersurface of a round sphere is a Clifford product

plain: After the equator, which soap-film surface inside a round sphere has the least area? A product of two spheres

beats.text: Schematically: the equator is the smallest minimal hypersurface of a round sphere
The candidates for second place are the Clifford products of two round spheres
The claim: every other minimal hypersurface has volume at least the smallest one, $a_m$

steps: Sweep the sphere with families of surfaces and track the largest
Marques and Neves did this for surfaces; extend it to all dimensions
Climb dimension by dimension, ruling out bad limits

achievement.label: Solomon–Yau conjecture (Yau's problem list)
achievement.context: Before: only $m = 2$, from Marques–Neves's proof of the Willmore conjecture
achievement.note: Min-max regularity in high dimensions is the delicate part

verify.ourCheck: We read the paper's strategy; we did not check the min-max argument

voice.text: The equator is the smallest minimal hypersurface of a round sphere. What comes second?
Sweep with families, then climb dimension by dimension, ruling out bad limits.
Claimed: a Clifford product of two spheres.

sources.quote: every closed connected minimal immersion into S^{m+1} with non-totally-geodesic image has volume (with multiplicity) at least a_m = min_k vol(Clifford product C_{k,m-k})
The equator is the smallest minimal hypersurface of a round sphere
The conjecture names the smallest minimal Clifford product $S^k(\sqrt{k/m}) \times S^{m-k}(\sqrt{(m-k)/m})$
Marques and Neves settled $m = 2$ through the Willmore conjecture
Min-max regularity in high dimensions is the delicate part. 32 pages, no Lean.
